newsitem.title: USA: Senate defeats balanced budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: Senate defeats balanced budget amendment.

text.p: The Republican-controlled Senate Tuesday rejected a proposed balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution which was opposed by President Clinton and most of the minority Democrats.

It failed on a 66 to 34 vote, one short of the two-thirds majority required. The amendment's Republican sponsors had expected the defeat and vowed to bring it to a vote again, saying it would be impossible to reduce the deficit without a constitutional requirement that the government balance its books each year.
All 55 Republicans and 11 of the 45 Democrats voted for the proposed amendment. It failed by one vote, just as it had in 1995, the year it came closest to passage.

If passed and ratified by 38 of 50 state legislatures, the amendment would require Washington to balance its budget every year during peacetime. It would take effect in 2002 or two years after ratification. Deficits would not be outlawed but it would take a three-fifths vote, a so-called super majority, to approve deficit spending and debt increases. It would also make it harder to raise taxes.

House leaders said they intended to take it up sometime this year, but they had looked to passage by the Senate to provide momentum in the House. The measure had become bogged down in that chamber, after Republican leaders became concerned Democrats might win a key change to exempt the politically popular Social Security program from deficit reduction.
